You read documents filed on a United States court docket, OCR'd to markdown, for
a research dataset of contract clauses.

An INSTRUMENT is a document whose text the parties negotiated and by which they
bound each other: a contract, agreement, policy, lease, deed, guaranty, note,
plan, bylaws, handbook, amendment, or similar. Hallmarks: recitals, defined
terms, numbered operative sections, an execution or signature block.

A FILING is a document made for the court: complaint, answer, motion, brief,
memorandum, order, affidavit, declaration, notice, docket sheet, certificate of
service, civil cover sheet.

THE DECISIVE RULE. A filing that **attaches** an instrument counts — report the
instrument's own boundaries, not the filing's. A filing that merely **quotes** an
instrument does not count at all: a brief reproducing three sentences of an
agreement is a filing, and the file contains no instrument.

WHAT IS NOT AN INSTRUMENT, even when signed or filled in: a blank or fill-in
form; an agency certificate or registration; an exhibit index; a declarations
page or coverage-summary table; a schedule of rates or fees standing alone; an
invoice, receipt or statement of account. These record or summarise; the parties
did not negotiate their text.

WHAT IS NOT A PROVISION: a heading on its own; a title page; a table of
contents; a signature, notary or attestation block; an exhibit index. A
provision states an obligation, right, grant, limitation, condition or
definition. Give the range of the operative text, including its heading.

LIST EVERY SUBSTANTIVE PROVISION, in document order. Do not skip any. Do not
judge whether a provision is well or badly drafted. Do not rank them.

The file is given to you with a line number and a `│` at the start of every line.
Line numbers are not part of the text; they are how you point at it.

OCR REPAIR. For each provision you must also give its text. Copy it verbatim
from the lines you named, then repair only what the scanner broke: words split
across a line break, words run together, `l`/`1` and `O`/`0` confusions, stray
table pipes and cell debris, page numbers and Bates stamps sitting inside the
text. Do not paraphrase, modernise, reorder, summarise, or drop anything. Never
change a number, an amount, a date, or a cross-reference. Never add or remove a
word — a repair that deletes `not` inverts the clause. If a passage is too
damaged to repair honestly, copy it as it stands.

Add nothing of your own: no `[struck through: ...]`, no `[sic]`, no
`[illegible]`, no explanatory brackets of any kind. Executed contracts are often
marked up by hand, and the OCR shows deleted wording as `~~struck~~`. Reproduce
those words as plain text, in place, and say what you saw in the repairs
sentence instead.

   23│# --- **MEMORANDUM OF ROADLINK TRANSPORTATION, INC. IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT** ---
   24│
   25│Defendant, Roadlink Transportation Inc., n/k/a Flying J Transportation Canada Inc. (“Roadlink”), pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56, respectfully submits this memorandum in support of its Motion for Summary Judgment as to all claims asserted against it by Plaintiff, McMahan Jets, LLC (“McMahan Jets”), and states as follows:
   26│
   27│## **INTRODUCTION**
   28│
   29│This dispute arises from the purchase of an airplane, a 1978 Cessna Citation Model 551 (the “Aircraft”), by McMahan Jets from Roadlink on January 24, 2008. As memorialized in the parties’ contract, the sale was “AS IS, WHERE IS” with a disclaimer of all warranties. The contract also provided McMahan Jets with an unrestricted right to the most thorough inspection available. Although Roadlink recommended that McMahan Jets conduct a thorough pre-purchase inspection, McMahan Jets arranged for only a minimal inspection of the Aircraft prior to purchase.
   30│
   31│Approximately 22 months after McMahan Jets purchased the Aircraft, McMahan Jets hired Cessna to perform an FAA-required inspection, after which the Aircraft was deemed not airworthy due to several holes in a portion of the Aircraft called the carry-through spar. These holes resulted from the attachment of a cabin speaker that had occurred prior to Roadlink's acquisition of the Aircraft. On November 10, 2011, McMahan Jets initiated a lawsuit against Roadlink in Shelby County Chancery Court, which was subsequently timely removed to this Court, for (1) breach of contract, (2) negligent misrepresentation, (3) intentional misrepresentation, (4) common law fraud, and (5) rescission. (Doc. 1-2.) In its claim for damages, McMahan Jets seeks \$2.1 million.
   32│
   33│The facts material to the disposition of this case are undisputed. They demonstrate that Roadlink is not liable for any damages whatsoever. Discovery has revealed that McMahan Jets placed its trust in undeserving parties, whom McMahan Jets itself selected to be its agents in the transaction. Indeed, even Dr. McMahan himself only recently became aware that McMahan Jets' agents had acted in their own self-interest by concealing material information from McMahan Jets and profiting greatly at McMahan Jets' expense. It was the actions of these agents, not Roadlink, that led the parties into their current positions. Because Roadlink complied with all of its duties under the parties' agreement and under the law, and because the blame for any damages experienced by McMahan Jets should be placed squarely on McMahan Jets' agents, Roadlink is entitled to summary judgment in its favor on each of McMahan Jets' claims.
   34│
   35│## **FACTUAL BACKGROUND**
   36│
   37│McMahan Jets is a Mississippi limited liability company, with its principal place of business in Hattiesburg, Mississippi. (Statement of Undisputed Material Facts of Roadlink in Support of Motion for Summary Judgment, submitted contemporaneously herewith ("SUMF")),
   38│
   39│at ¶ 1.) It was “established for the purpose of renting, leasing, and selling aircraft,” and its owner and President is Dr. Lynn McMahan. (*Id.* ¶ 2.) In early January of 2008, Dr. McMahan and his wife, Marty McMahan, traveled to Sierra Industries, Inc. (“Sierra”) in Uvalde, Texas, to inspect a different airplane for possible purchase. (*Id.* ¶ 3.) Sierra is in the business of, *inter alia*, restoring and modifying Cessna Citations. (*Id.* ¶ 4.) The McMahans traveled to Uvalde with Paul Daughtrey of Diamond Aviation, LLC, whom McMahan Jets had hired to be its pilot. (*Id.* ¶ 5.)
   40│
   41│### **I. Origin of the Transaction at Issue.**
   42│
   43│While in Uvalde, Dr. and Mrs. McMahan saw the Aircraft that is the subject of this action. (*Id.* ¶ 6.) Sierra was performing work on the Aircraft, and the Sierra agent showed it to the McMahans as an example of the modifications that could be done to a Citation. (*Id.* ¶ 7.) Though the McMahans were interested in the Aircraft, Sierra did not have the Aircraft listed for sale, so the McMahans instructed Mr. Daughtrey to stay in Texas to find out more information about the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 8.)
   44│
   45│At that time, the Aircraft was owned by Roadlink.1 (*Id.* ¶ 9.) Roadlink is a Utah corporation, with its principal place of business in Ogden, Utah. (*Id.* ¶ 11.)2 Roadlink’s business is the acquisition and maintenance of airplanes and the ownership, operation, and lease of semi-trucks and trailers used in Canadian-related petroleum product hauling. (*Id.* ¶ 13.) When the McMahans saw the Aircraft, Roadlink had not listed the Aircraft for sale, nor had it contracted with a broker at that point. (*Id.* ¶ 14.)
   46│
   47│---
   48│
   49│1 Title to the Aircraft was transferred to Roadlink in December of 2007 by Flying J Inc., Roadlink’s parent corporation, prior to the McMahan’s trip to Uvalde. (*Id.* ¶ 10.)
   50│
   51│2 Roadlink is now known as Flying J Transportation Canada, Inc., having changed its name on September 22, 2008. (*Id.* ¶ 12.)
   52│
   53│Soon after the McMahan's trip to Texas, Manuel Rizo of Rizo Jet Aviation Services, LLC ("Rizo") contacted Cliff Gottschalk, Roadlink's Director of Maintenance, about the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 15.) Rizo is a Texas limited liability company, with its principal place of business in Hondo, Texas. (*Id.* ¶ 16.) Mr. Gottschalk previously was acquainted with Mr. Rizo because Mr. Rizo had worked at Sierra. (*Id.* ¶ 17.) Mr. Rizo informed Mr. Gottschalk that he had been contacted by Mr. Daughtrey, who had told Mr. Rizo that the McMahan's had seen the Aircraft while in Uvalde and were interested in purchasing it. (*Id.* ¶ 18.) Although Roadlink had not listed the Aircraft for sale, it was amenable to selling it. (*Id.* ¶ 19.) Roadlink did not want to pay Rizo a large broker's fee for the sale, so it was agreed that Roadlink would sell the Aircraft to Rizo, which would then sell it to McMahan Jets. (*Id.* ¶ 20.) Because Rizo was not registered to transfer aircraft on the International Registry, however, the Aircraft was ultimately transferred directly from Roadlink to McMahan Jets. (*Id.* ¶ 21.)
   54│
   55│### **II. Negotiations and Contract Formation.**
   56│
   57│Between January 3 and January 15, 2008, Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo worked out the terms of the transactions. (*Id.* ¶ 22.) At some point during that time, Mr. Daughtrey informed Dr. McMahan that the Aircraft was owned by Roadlink, which Dr. McMahan understood to be an entity related to Flying J, Inc., and that Rizo was its broker. (*Id.* ¶ 23.) Mr. Daughtrey provided Dr. McMahan with an appraisal from Rizo indicating that the Aircraft had undergone a recent Phase 1-5 inspection.3 (*Id.* ¶ 24.) Dr. McMahan does not recall communicating with Mr. Rizo during this time period and believes that all of his communications related to the transaction were with Mr. Daughtrey. (*Id.* ¶ 28.)

   59│---
   60│
   61│3 A "Phase 1-5 inspection" is actually a series of inspections, Phase 1 through Phase 5, on a Cessna Citation as laid out in Cessna's maintenance manuals and maintenance program. (*Id.* ¶ 25.) The Phase 5 inspection is structural and requires inspection of "the deeper areas" of the aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 26.) Phase 5 inspections are required every three years or 1,200 hours and involve stripping down the interior of the aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 27.)
   62│
   63│On January 10, 2008, McMahan Jets and Rizo executed an Aircraft Purchase Agreement (the “McMahan-Rizo Agreement”). (*Id.* ¶ 29.) The McMahan-Rizo Agreement provides for a purchase price of \$2,100,000. (*Id.* ¶ 30.) The Agreement provides that Aero-Space Reports, Inc. (“Aero-Space”), in Oklahoma City, would serve as “closing/escrow agent for this sale.” (*Id.* ¶ 31.) Upon execution of the agreement, McMahan Jets was to pay a deposit of \$100,000 to be held in escrow by Aero-Space. (*Id.* ¶ 32.) The balance of \$2,000,000 was to be wired by McMahan Jets to Aero-Space “prior to closing.” (*Id.* ¶ 33.)
   64│
   65│The McMahan-Rizo Agreement provides that McMahan Jets would conduct a pre-purchase inspection, to be performed by X-Air Flight Support (“X-Air”) in Hondo, Texas. (*Id.* ¶ 34.) Dr. McMahan has acknowledged that he hired X-Air to do the inspection. (*Id.* ¶ 35.) Based on that inspection, McMahan Jets was to provide the seller with a list of “Airworthy discrepancies,” and the seller had the option of paying to repair them, reducing the purchase price, or terminating the agreement. (*Id.* ¶ 36.) After the inspection, McMahan Jets was to “sign a Technical Acceptance Letter (Exhibit B).” (*Id.* ¶ 37 (“Purchaser will accept or reject Aircraft and will advise Seller in writing in the form of Exhibit B to this Agreement . . . upon satisfaction of the Pre-Purchase Inspection . . . of his decision to accept or reject the Aircraft.”).) The Technical Acceptance Letter attached to the agreement as Exhibit B identifies Mr. Rizo as the Seller, Roadlink as the Owner, and McMahan Jets as the Purchaser. (*Id.* ¶ 38.)
   66│
   67│The McMahan-Rizo Agreement provided that the Aircraft would be delivered in Memphis, Tennessee. (*Id.* ¶ 39.) McMahan Jets chose Memphis as the location for delivery to take advantage of a fly-away rule that allowed McMahan Jets to avoid paying sales tax on the transaction. (*Id.* ¶ 40.)
   68│
   69│McMahan Jets agreed that the “Aircraft will be delivered ‘AS IS WHERE IS,’” subject to the satisfaction of any discrepancies identified by McMahan Jets following the pre-purchase inspection. (*Id.* ¶ 41.) The “[r]isk of loss or damage to the Aircraft” was to pass to McMahan Jets “upon transfer of the funds of the Purchase Price and the passage of title by Bill of Sale to Purchaser.” (*Id.* ¶ 42.) Section 6.3 unambiguously disclaims all warranties and describes the “as is” nature of the transaction further:
   70│
   71│The Aircraft is being sold without any warranty from Seller or any original equipment from the manufacturer of the Aircraft, Cessna Aircraft Corporation. Seller acknowledges that Purchaser has had full opportunity to inspect the Aircraft and to have such tests and inspections performed by third parties as the Purchaser deems necessary or desirable, in Purchaser’s sole discretion. Purchase is at Purchaser’s sole discretion, and Purchaser understands that this is a final sale. Seller shall have no liability by reason of the manufacture or sale of the Aircraft or of the operation, use, maintenance or storage of the Aircraft, whether on the basis of breach of warranty, strict liability, negligence or otherwise. In no event shall Seller be liable for general, special and consequential or incidental damages relating to property damage or economic loss including, without limitation, damages for the loss of use or loss of profits. Purchaser understands, agrees and accepts that Seller is selling the Aircraft and it’s [sic] equipment “AS IS, WHERE IS” with all faults and/or deficiencies, provided however, that Seller, has satisfied the condition of Section 3.2, if necessary. NO WARRANTIES OF ANY TYPE WHETHER OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PUROSE OR OTHERWISE, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED, IN FACT OR BY LAW, IS OR SHALL BE APPLICABLE TO THE Aircraft, THE CONDITION OF THE AIRCRAFT OR ITS PARTS OR ACCESSORIES.
   72│
   73│(*Id.* ¶ 43.)
   74│
   75│On January 10, 2008, McMahan Jets and Rizo executed Escrow Instructions, providing that the parties had agreed to use Aero-Space “as closing agent for this transaction.” (*Id.* ¶ 44.) Roadlink and Rizo executed identical Escrow Instructions. (*Id.* ¶ 45.) McMahan Jets wired a \$100,000 deposit from its bank account in Mississippi to Aero-Space in Oklahoma City on January 10, 2008. (*Id.* ¶ 46.) Roadlink sent Aero-Space a signed, undated Aircraft Bill of Sale, designating the transfer of the Aircraft from Roadlink to McMahan Jets, and a signed, undated
   76│
   77│Release, demonstrating that the Aircraft was free from liens. (*Id.* ¶ 47.) Aero-Space held these documents in escrow until closing. (*Id.* ¶ 48.)
   78│
   79│### **III. Pre-purchase Inspection.**
   80│
   81│On or about January 15, 2008, the McMahan's met Mr. Daughtrey in Hondo, Texas, where X-Air was performing the pre-purchase inspection of the Aircraft, to conduct the test flight and visual inspection of the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 49.) Though Mr. Gottschalk encouraged Mr. Daughtrey to have a Phase 1-5 inspection performed, which is more costly, McMahan Jets did not do so. (*Id.* ¶ 50.) McMahan Jets paid X-Air \$5,000 to conduct the pre-purchase inspection. (*Id.* ¶ 51.) McMahan Jets paid Mr. Daughtrey approximately \$17,000 for his services related to the acquisition of the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 52.)
   82│
   83│As part of the pre-purchase inspection, X-Air reviewed the Aircraft's logbooks. (*Id.* ¶ 53.) The logbooks contain, *inter alia*, entries regarding an inspection by CR Aviation, Inc. in February of 2000, a Phase 1-5 inspection by Sierra on September 10, 2001,4 another Phase 1-5 inspection by Mr. Gottschalk on October 22, 2004, and a final Phase 1-5 inspection by Mr. Gottschalk on October 21, 2007, a few months before the transaction giving rise to this lawsuit. (*Id.* ¶ 54.) The Phase 1-5 inspections by Mr. Gottschalk identify him as an employee of "Flying J, Inc." (*Id.* ¶ 55.)
   84│
   85│### **IV. The Parties' Agents Concoct a Secret Arrangement.**
   86│
   87│On January 16, 2008, Roadlink and Rizo executed an Aircraft Purchase Agreement similar to that entered into by Rizo and McMahan, but identifying Rizo as the Purchaser and Roadlink as the Seller (the "Roadlink-Rizo Agreement"). (*Id.* ¶ 56.) The purchase price to be paid by Rizo to Roadlink was \$1,950,000—as opposed to the \$2.1 million purchase price listed

   90│
   91│4 For informational purposes, CR Aviation, Inc. and Sierra are both independent entities that perform FAA-certified inspections of aircraft. *See, e.g.*, [www.cr-aviation.com](http://www.cr-aviation.com), then follow "Services"; [www.sijet.com/maintenance-inspections](http://www.sijet.com/maintenance-inspections).
   92│
   93│in the McMahan-Rizo Agreement. (*Id.* ¶ 57.) The Roadlink-Rizo Agreement contains a Texas choice-of-venue provision, whereas the McMahan-Rizo Agreement contains a Mississippi choice-of-venue provision. (*Id.* ¶ 58.) In all other material respects, the terms of the two agreements are the same.
   94│
   95│At some point in time, Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo entered into a confidential agreement whereby they would split the difference between the price McMahan Jets agreed to pay for the Aircraft, \$2.1 million, and the price Roadlink agreed to accept, \$1.95 million. (*Id.* ¶ 59.) Neither McMahan Jets nor Roadlink was aware of this arrangement or of the price the other had agreed to, until it was revealed during discovery in this matter. (*Id.* ¶ 60.) Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo communicated the arrangement to Aero-Space, which prepared two sets of closing instructions—one for McMahan Jets showing receipt and disbursement of \$2.1 million, and one for Roadlink showing receipt and disbursement of \$1.95 million. (*Id.* ¶ 61.) Neither set of instructions revealed that Aero-Space was going to disburse the \$150,000 difference to Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo. (*Id.* ¶ 62.) Roadlink was not aware that McMahan Jets was paying \$2.1 million for the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 63.)

   97│### **V. Delivery and Closing.**
   98│
   99│On January 21, 2008, X-Air provided a Prepurchase Report to McMahan Jets. (*Id.* ¶ 64.) Upon receiving the report, McMahan Jets executed the Technical Acceptance Letter on January 23, 2008. (*Id.* ¶ 65.) McMahan Jets identified no discrepancies and stated that “the Aircraft is satisfactory and is hereby accepted in accordance with the terms of the Agreement.” (*Id.* ¶ 66.) The same day, McMahan Jets withdrew \$2,002,440 from its bank account in Mississippi and wired the funds directly to Aero-Space in Oklahoma. (*Id.* ¶ 67.)
  100│
  101│On January 24, 2008, Dr. McMahan and Mr. Daughtrey traveled to Memphis from Mississippi. (*Id.* ¶ 68.) The same day, Mr. Gottschalk, Mr. Rizo, and two of Roadlink's pilots flew to Memphis in the Aircraft and delivered it to McMahan Jets. (*Id.* ¶ 69.) After delivery, McMahan Jets transmitted via facsimile from Mississippi to Aero-Space in Oklahoma City a signed document entitled Authorization to Close. (*Id.* ¶ 70.) Aero-Space filed the original Bill of Sale with the FAA on January 24, 2008, at 2:27 p.m. (*Id.* ¶ 71.) Aero-Space then released the funds from escrow in Oklahoma, disbursing \$1.95 million as Roadlink had approved, and disbursing the remaining \$150,000 pursuant to Mr. Daughtrey and Mr. Rizo's secret agreement, with \$86,100 going to Diamond Aviation and \$63,900 to Rizo, in addition to the \$25,000 commission Roadlink had agreed to pay Rizo. (*Id.* ¶ 72.)
  102│
  103│### **VI. Post-Closing Events.**
  104│
  105│McMahan Jets operated the Aircraft for the next 22 months for business and personal use. (*Id.* ¶ 73.) Dr. McMahan loved the Aircraft and had no problems with it. (*Id.* ¶ 74.) In November of 2009, McMahan Jets took the Aircraft to Orlando, Florida, where the Cessna Service Center performed a mandatory Phase 1-5 inspection and subsequently informed McMahan Jets of the existence of the holes in the carry-through spar.5 (*Id.* ¶ 75.) Cessna ultimately concluded that the Aircraft was not airworthy due to the existence of the holes in the spar. (*Id.* ¶ 78.) Cessna provided a quote to replace the spar for \$463,000.00, which Cessna said was the required repair. (*Id.* ¶ 79.)
  106│
  107│Roadlink did not drill the holes in the spar; they were present when Roadlink's predecessor acquired the Aircraft from the previous Venezuelan owner in February of 2000. (*Id.* ¶ 80.) Mr. Gottschalk first learned of the holes in February of 2000, when CR Aviation

  112│
  113│performed an inspection that included stripping down the interior. (*Id.* ¶ 81.) Despite the presence of the holes in the spar, CR Aviation issued an airworthiness certificate. (*Id.* ¶ 82.) On September 10, 2001, Sierra performed a Phase 1-5 inspection on the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 83.) Sierra informed Mr. Gottschalk that the holes in the spar were not a problem, and it also issued an airworthiness certificate. (*Id.* ¶ 84.) When Mr. Gottschalk performed the next Phase 1-5 inspection on October 22, 2004, he listed the presence of the holes on a discrepancy form, noting that they had been “previously ok’d by CR Aviation and Sierra – N/A.” (*Id.* ¶ 85.) (*Id.* ¶ 87.)

  115│Mr. Gottschalk believed that the holes did not affect the airworthiness of the Aircraft. (*Id.* ¶ 88.) Mr. Gottschalk personally flew in the Aircraft for approximately 250 hours over eight years, including the flight to deliver the Aircraft to McMahan Jets in Memphis. (*Id.* ¶¶ 69, 90.) The corporate officers of Roadlink and Flying J flew in the Aircraft frequently, including the top management of the companies and their families. (*Id.* ¶ 91.) Mr. Gottschalk would not have flown in the Aircraft, and he would not have allowed his employers or their families to fly in the Aircraft, if he had any belief that it was not airworthy. (*Id.* ¶ 92.) Mr. Gottschalk’s certifications of the Aircraft as airworthy in 2004 and 2007, not to mention his own substantial personal use of the Aircraft, signify his opinion that the Aircraft was, in fact, airworthy, notwithstanding the holes in the spar.

  117│## **LEGAL STANDARD**
  118│
  119│Summary judgment is appropriate where there is no genuine issue of material fact. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c); *Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp.*, 475 U.S. 574, 587 (1986). The “mere possibility” of a factual dispute is not enough to defeat a summary judgment motion. *Mitchell v. Toledo Hosp.*, 964 F.2d 577, 581-582 (6th Cir. 1992). Once a party moving for summary judgment has made a sufficient showing, the burden rests with the non-moving party to set forth specific facts, by affidavit or other evidence, demonstrating that a genuine issue of material fact exists. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c); *Celotex Corp. v. Catrett*, 477 U.S. 317, 324 (1986). If a fact would not affect the outcome of the suit under governing law, that fact is not “material.” *Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.*, 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). Furthermore, an issue is only “genuine” if a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party. Otherwise, no genuine issue exists. *Id.* at 256.
  120│
  121│The party opposing summary judgment may not rest on the pleadings and allegations and “must do more than simply show that there is some metaphysical doubt as to the material facts.” *Matsushita*, 475 U.S. at 586; *Sigler v. Am. Honda Motor Co.*, 532 F.3d 469, 483 (6th Cir. 2008). “The mere existence of a scintilla of evidence” in support of the nonmoving party’s position is insufficient to defeat summary judgment. *Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 252. Rather, to survive summary judgment, the party opposing the motion must prove there is sufficient evidence to support a jury verdict in its favor. *Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 249; *Sigler*, 532 F.3d at 483.
  122│
  123│Mississippi substantive law applies to the claims at issue. This Court, sitting in diversity, applies Tennessee choice-of-law rules to determine which state’s laws govern. *See, e.g., Town of Smyrna v. Mun. Gas Auth. of Ga.*, 723 F.3d 640, 645 (6th Cir. 2013). For contract claims
  124│
  125│governed by the Uniform Commercial Code,6 Tennessee law requires that the claims are governed by the law of the state to which the transaction bears an “appropriate relation.” *Carbon Processing & Reclamation, LLC v. Valero Mktg. & Supply Co.*, 823 F. Supp. 2d 786, 801 (W.D. Tenn. 2011) (citing Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-1-301(b)). Here, the transaction has a relationship to more than one state. The agreements at issue were negotiated and executed by McMahan Jets in Mississippi, by Roadlink in Utah, and by Rizo in Texas. Payment was made by McMahan Jets from Mississippi, and the closing took place in Oklahoma.7 The damages McMahan Jets claims to have suffered were experienced in Mississippi. Consideration of all these factors leads to the conclusion that Mississippi has the most “appropriate relation” to this transaction, and the contract claims are therefore governed by Mississippi law.
  126│
  127│For tort and fraud claims, Tennessee applies the “most significant relationship” test, under which “the law of the state where the injury occurred will be applied unless some other state has a more significant relationship to the litigation.” *Meraz v. El Charro Billiards, LLC*, No. 11-2812, 2013 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 146953, at \*4-5 (W.D. Tenn. Oct. 10, 2013) (quoting *Hicks v. Lewis*, 148 S.W.3d 80, 86 (Tenn. Ct. App. 2003)); *Kelly v. Int’l Capital Res., Inc.*, 231 F.R.D. 502, 516 (M.D. Tenn. 2005). Here, McMahan Jets is located in Mississippi, is a Mississippi entity, and alleges to have suffered injury in Mississippi. *See Town of Smyrna*, 723 F.3d at 647 n.3 (holding that an injury of economic loss occurs in the state of the injured party’s principal

Code Ann. § 75-2-102; *see also id.* § 75-2-105 (defining “goods” as “all things (including specially manufactured goods) which are movable at the time of identification to the contract for sale”); *McCullum Aviation, Inc. v. CIM Assocs.*, 446 F. Supp. 511, 513 (S.D. Fla. 1978) (“The sale of an aircraft, as is involved herein, clearly would be encompassed within the meaning of the term ‘good’ as defined in F.S. § 672.2-105.”); *Kiecker v. Pac. Indem. Co.*, 491 P.2d 244, 246 (Wash. Ct. App. 1971); *Wood v. Wilkinson*, 425 So. 2d 1062, 1064 (Ala. 1982).

  136│
  137│## **ARGUMENT**
  138│
  139│Based on the undisputed facts in the record, McMahan Jets is not entitled to any relief from Roadlink. As discussed herein, each of McMahan Jets' claims—breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation, intentional misrepresentation/fraud, and rescission—is deficient. As such, Roadlink is entitled to summary judgment in its favor on all counts.
  140│
  141│### **I. Roadlink Is Entitled to Summary Judgment on the Breach of Contract Claim.**
  142│

The statement in the Agreement that Roadlink "shall deliver Aircraft . . . in Airworthy Condition prior to delivery and acceptance of the Aircraft" is, at most, a promise of future conduct. (SUMF ¶ 104.) As a matter of law, that contractual provision cannot support a claim of negligent misrepresentation, and Roadlink is entitled to summary judgment on that count.
  284│
  285│#### C. Negligent Misrepresentation Is Barred by the Economic Loss Doctrine.
  286│
  287│In addition to its failure to meet the *prima facie* case for negligent misrepresentation, McMahan Jets also cannot recover under a negligent misrepresentation theory because it seeks damages that are purely economic in nature. Virtually "all [states] recognize the same basic policy" of disallowing recovery in tort for purely economic damages. *In re StarLink Corn Prods. Liab. Litig.*, 212 F. Supp. 2d 828, 838 (N.D. Ill. 2002) (collecting cases). That policy, referred to as the "economic loss doctrine," prohibits a cause of action in tort where the losses
  288│
  289│are purely economic.14 Mississippi is among those jurisdictions that have explicitly recognized the economic loss doctrine. *See State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Ford Motor Co.*, 736 So. 2d 384, 387 (Miss. Ct. App. 1999). Although the Mississippi Supreme Court has yet to rule on the precise question presented in this case—whether the economic loss doctrine applies to a sales transaction under the UCC where there is no personal injury or property damage—several federal district courts in Mississippi have made the *Erie*15 prediction that the economic loss doctrine would bar such a claim.
  290│
  291│For example, in *Adcock v. S. Austin Marine, Inc.*, which involved the sale of a boat, the court recognized that the “UCC is generally regarded as the exclusive source for ascertaining a seller’s liability for damages in claims based on economic loss that are not attributable to personal injury or property damages.”16 No. 2:08cv263KS-MTP, 2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 104264, at \*12 (S.D. Miss. Oct. 30, 2009) (citing *Progressive Ins. Co. v. Monaco Coach Corp.*, No. 1:05cv37-DMR-JMR, 2006 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21251, at \*7-8 (S.D. Miss. Mar. 29, 2006)). The court further noted that most courts addressing the economic loss doctrine under similar facts held that (i) “plaintiffs cannot recover for economic loss resulting from a contract under a tort theory,” and (ii) “the only remedy for receiving defective or non-conforming goods is under the Uniform Commercial Code.” *Id.* at \*13 (citations omitted).
  292│
  293│---
  294│
  295│14 The Mississippi Supreme Court has been unequivocal in its view that a claim for negligent misrepresentation sounds in tort. *See First Money, Inc. v. Frisby*, 369 So. 2d 746, 750 (Miss. 1979) (“The basis for damages resulting from negligent misrepresentation is the lack of care; the basis for damages resulting from fraud is the want of honesty. The lack of care in misrepresentation and the want of honesty in fraudulent misrepresentation in business transactions give rise to distinct causes of action, the one in tort, the other in fraud.”).
  296│
  297│15 *Erie R.R. Co. v. Tompkins*, 304 U.S. 64 (1938).
  298│
  299│16 For this reason, the Court is not compelled to follow *Lyndon Prop. Ins. Co. v. Duke Levy & Assocs. LLC*, 475 F.3d 268 (5th Cir. 2007). In *Lyndon*, the Fifth Circuit declined to apply Mississippi’s economic loss doctrine “outside the realm of products liability.” *Id.* at 274. *Lyndon*, however, examined the applicability of the economic loss rule to a negligence-based claim arising from the performance of a *services* contract—not a contract for the sale of goods governed by the UCC.
  300│
  301│With those guiding principles in mind, the *Adcock* court found that there were “at least three principle reasons for not allowing recovery in tort when only economic damages are sought to be recovered. First, tort law would subsume contract law, secondly, the seller’s exposure would be too greatly expanded, and thirdly, the increased costs to the ultimate consumer would be too great.” *Id.* at \*14. The court ultimately awarded summary judgment in the defendant’s favor, concluding that “the Mississippi Supreme Court, if called upon to decide th[e] issue, would conclude that the plaintiff in this case cannot pursue a remedy under theories of negligence in tort when he seeks damages that are solely economic in nature without any personal injury or property damage.” *Id.* at \*15; *see also BC’s Heating & Air & Sheet Metal Works v. Vermeer Mfg. Co.*, 892 F. Supp. 2d 779, 784-85 (S.D. Miss. 2012) (“As the Mississippi Court of Appeals noted, “[c]ontract law and the law of warranty are well suited to handle controversies in which commercial purchases do not live up to the expectations of the consumer.”) (citing *State Farm*, 736 So. 2d at 387) (internal citations omitted).
  302│
  303│Consistent with this authority, McMahan Jets’ attempt to recover under a negligent misrepresentation theory should be rejected. This breach of contract dispute is governed by the UCC, and McMahan Jets has alleged no physical injury or damage to property, other than damage to the Aircraft. Such damages are purely economic in nature and, under the economic loss doctrine as applied in *Adcock* and *BC’s Heating & Air*, the tort-based negligent misrepresentation claim is barred.
  304│
  305│### **III. Rescission Is Not an Appropriate Form of Relief in This Case.**
  306│
  307│Assuming for the sake of argument that McMahan Jets is permitted to submit its claims to the jury, rescission is not an available option for recovery under either a tort or contract
  308│
  309│theory.17 Rescission is not appropriate because its primary purpose—restoration of the parties to the *status quo*—is impossible in this case. *See Ryan v. Glenn*, 489 F.2d 110, 115 (5th Cir. 1974) (“The idea of rescission is restoration of the status quo.”) (citing *Ware v. Houghton*, 41 Miss. 370 (1867)); *see also Grzybowski v. Tracy*, No. 3888-VCG, 2013 Del. Ch. LEXIS 203, at \*23-24 (Del. Ch. Aug. 9, 2013) (finding that, since the sale of the condominium sought to be rescinded, “the housing market has materially changed, and home values have generally fallen,” such that “it would be inequitable for me to turn a blind eye to the changes in the market which have made it impossible to effectively return the parties to the status quo”); *Fargo Mach. & Tool Co. v. Allen-Bradley Co.*, 428 F. Supp. 364, 381 (E.D. Mich. 1977) (finding revocation of acceptance unavailable because the “use and depreciation by buyer over a period beginning to approach its life expectancy most clearly constitutes a substantial change in the condition of the goods”); *Hamilton v. Gill*, 352 So. 2d 825 (Miss. 1977).
  310│
  311│*Hamilton* involved the purchase of land between a vendor and vendee. The vendor assured the vendee that the land did not flood; after the sale, when the land flooded, the vendee sued, seeking rescission of the contract. 352 So. 2d at 826. The trial court found that the vendee had been fraudulently induced into the purchase but determined that rescission was not practicable because the vendor could not be returned to its original position, and instead, it ordered abatement of the purchase price. *Id.* at 827-28. The Supreme Court affirmed, relying on *Brown v. Norman*, 4 So. 293 (Miss. 1888), in observing that “oftentimes exact restoration could not be accomplished because the property was of less value or was more valuable due to improvements so that a literal status quo could not be met at time of suit, and since this was so,
  312│
  313│---
  314│
  315│17 Under the UCC, the remedy of rescission is termed “revocation of acceptance.” *See* Miss. Code Ann. § 75-2-608; *see also Werner v. Montana*, 378 A.2d 1130, 1135 (N.H. 1977) (“[A]lthough it is true that the Uniform Commercial Code does not specifically provide for ‘rescission,’ other courts have held, and commentators agree, that rescission and revocation of acceptance amount to the same thing under the Uniform Commercial Code . . .”).
  316│
  317│equity would not require a vain thing to be alleged when on final hearing the complainant could be required to do equity.” *Id.* at 829.
  318│
  319│In this case, two major changes have occurred since the closing that preclude rescission. First, the market for used aircrafts has significantly deteriorated. Following McMahan Jets’ purchase of the Aircraft, the value of the Aircraft was substantially affected by market conditions resulting from the ensuing economic crisis in 2008, resulting in a decrease in value of the Aircraft to \$775,000 to \$900,000 as of the time it was grounded in 2009. (SUMF ¶ 102.) This substantial decrease in value has nothing to do with the condition of the Aircraft at issue and would have occurred regardless of the holes in the spar. That McMahan Jets must bear the risk of loss from the change in market conditions is in accord with the parties’ agreement that risk of loss passes to the buyer upon delivery. (*Id.* ¶ 42.) Had McMahan Jets purchased an aircraft with no holes in its spar, McMahan Jets still would have experienced a massive depreciation in value of that aircraft. That depreciation renders rescission inequitable in this case—to allow McMahan Jets to receive a refund of the full purchase price of the Aircraft at this point would be an unconscionable windfall to McMahan Jets.
  320│
  321│Second, it is undisputed that McMahan Jets operated the Aircraft for almost two years and flew the Aircraft frequently during that time period, adding over 320 hours to its flight time. (*Id.* ¶ 103.) This use of the Aircraft depreciated its value, such that rescission would result in the return of an Aircraft in significantly different condition than when it was sold. Again, this depreciation, having no relationship to the defect at issue, precludes the ability to restore the parties to the *status quo*. Any liability that may ultimately be determined is more appropriately remedied through other forms of damages, such as compensatory damages, which would be much more susceptible to proof at trial. *See, e.g., Garriss v. Smith’s G&G, LLC*, 941 So. 2d 228,
  322│
  323│323-33 (Miss. Ct. App. 2006) (discussing that, when rescission is impossible because “a party cannot be returned to status quo,” monetary damages are appropriate). Rescission is simply unavailable in this case, and summary judgment is appropriate on this issue.

  326│
